The Little bee-eater Merops pusillus exhibits a distinct life-history strategy shaped by its Afro-tropical distribution and insectivorous diet. The initial wet weight of a freshly laid egg, measured in a series from nests in Tanzania, is approximately 2.7 grams [Ww0 = approximately 2.7 grams]. This modest egg mass is followed by a slightly lower wet weight at birth of 2.5 grams [Wwb = 2.5 grams] for the newly hatched nestling, a pattern consistent with altricial development in related meropids. Females typically produce a single clutch of 2 to 3 eggs per nest [N_R_i = 2 to 3 eggs per nest] and raise approximately one brood per year [F_R_i = approximately one brood per year], a modest annual reproductive output that reflects the prolonged period of parental care required by these cavity-nesting birds. Under ambient thermal conditions common to their breeding grounds (40 °C [T = 40 °C]), the reproductive physiology of this species appears finely tuned to high temperatures.

Incubation dynamics in this species reveal a notable temperature sensitivity during embryonic development. Eggs maintained at a constant 36 °C [T = 36 °C] hatch after 19 days [ab = 19 days], an incubation period that aligns well with values reported for the congener Merops apiaster, which requires three to four weeks. This relatively short incubation is compensated by intense parental feeding during the nestling phase. The fledgling period is complete when the young take their first flight at 23.5 days after hatching [tx = 23.5 days after hatching], measured under field conditions where daily maximum temperatures often reach 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This rapid transition from hatching to flight capability is characteristic of small-bodied bee-eaters and allows the altricial chicks, which weigh around 2.5 grams [Wwb = around 2.5 grams] at emergence, to escape the confines of the burrow nest quickly compared to larger meropids.

Sexual maturation in Merops pusillus follows a schedule that is comparatively accelerated for a bird of its body mass. Under the warm thermal regime characteristic of their open savannah habitats, where midday air temperatures routinely approach 40 °C [T = 40 °C], young bee-eaters reach puberty at 70.5 days after hatching [tp = 70.5 days after hatching]. This remarkably early age at gonadal activation far exceeds the pace seen in many temperate-zone passerines of similar adult size. The ultimate wet weight of 14.8 grams [Wwi = 14.8 grams] is attained by breeding adults, a body mass that positions this species among the smaller-bodied members of the genus Merops. The attainment of this adult mass prior to first reproduction appears critical, as the energetic demands of excavating nesting burrows and provisioning offspring require substantial somatic reserves.

The timing of the first successful brood provides insight into the species’ life-history trade-offs. First reproduction occurs at 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching] when individuals are maintained under average environmental temperatures of 40 °C [T = 40 °C], representing a full calendar year of growth and experience before the onset of breeding. This delay is almost certainly linked to the prolonged period required for the acquisition of essential foraging skills and the establishment of a breeding territory. In contrast to many smaller passerines that breed in their first spring, the little bee-eater defers first reproduction until its second year, a pattern that resembles the life-history strategy observed in the congeneric species Merops bullockoides. Maximum longevity in the wild has been estimated at 7 years [am = 7 years], based on mark-recapture studies in southern Africa conducted at sites where thermal conditions often reach 40 °C [T = 40 °C].

Comparative analysis of the little bee-eater’s life-history data with those of its congeners reveals distinct phylogenetic and ecological patterns. The initial wet egg mass of 2.7 grams [Ww0 = 2.7 grams] is proportionally smaller than that of the larger European bee-eater Merops apiaster, reflecting an allometric scaling of egg size with female body mass. The nestlings, weighing just 2.5 grams [Wwb = 2.5 grams] at hatching, undergo a period of rapid mass gain, ultimately reaching 14.8 grams [Wwi = 14.8 grams] as adults, which represents roughly a six-fold increase from hatchling mass. The relatively brief fledging interval of 23.5 days after hatching [tx = 23.5 days after hatching] observed under the species’ typical thermal conditions (40 °C [T = 40 °C]) is critical for minimizing nest predation risk in the exposed savannah environment. Overall, the life-history of this diminutive bee-eater is characterized by a late onset of first reproduction at one year after hatching [tR = one year after hatching] and a maximum lifespan of 7 years [am = 7 years], traits that together define a moderately slow pace of life for a bird of just 14.8 grams [Wwi = 14.8 grams] at a temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C].
